chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Prince Andrew reached army headquarters at the end of June. The first army, with which was the Emperor, occupied the fortified camp at Drissa; the second army was retreating, trying to join up with the first, from which it was said to be cut off by large French forces. Everyone was dissatisfied with the general course of affairs in the Russian army, but no one anticipated any danger of invasion of the Russian provinces, and no one thought the war would extend farther than the western, Polish, provinces.

Prince Andrew found Barclay de Tolly, to whom he had been assigned, on the bank of the Drissa. As there was not a single town or large village in the vicinity of the camp, the immense number of generals and courtiers accompanying the army were living in the best houses of villages on both sides of the river, over a radius of six miles. Barclay de Tolly was quartered nearly three miles from the Emperor. He received Bolkonsky stiffly and coldly and told him in his foreign accent that he would mention him to the Emperor for a decision on his assignment, but asked him meanwhile to remain on his staff. Anatole Kuragin, whom Prince Andrew had hoped to find with the army, was not there. He had gone to Petersburg, but Prince Andrew was glad to hear this. His mind was occupied with the affairs of the great center that was conducting a gigantic war, and he was glad to be free for a while from the distraction caused by thoughts of Kuragin. During the first four days, while no duties were required of him, Prince Andrew rode all around the fortified camp and, using his own knowledge and his conversations with experts, tried to form a definite opinion about it. But the question of whether the camp was advantageous or not remained unresolved in his mind. Already from his military experience and from what he had seen in the Austrian campaign, he had reached the conclusion that in war the most carefully considered plans have no significance and that everything depends on how unexpected movements of the enemy — which cannot be foreseen — are met, and on how and by whom the whole matter is handled. To understand this last point, Prince Andrew, using his position and connections, tried to grasp the character of the army's leadership and of the men and factions involved, and he arrived at the following picture of the situation.

While the Emperor had still been at Vilna, the forces had been divided into three armies. First, the army under Barclay de Tolly; second, the army under Bagration; and third, the one commanded by Tormasov. The Emperor was with the first army, but not as commander in chief. In the orders issued, it was not stated that the Emperor would take command, only that he would be with the army. The Emperor moreover had with him not a commander in chief's staff but the imperial headquarters staff. In attendance on him was the head of the imperial staff, Quartermaster General Prince Volkonsky, as well as generals, imperial aides-de-camp, diplomatic officials, and a large number of foreigners — but not the army staff. Besides these, there were in attendance on the Emperor without any definite assignments: Arakcheev, the former Minister of War; Count Bennigsen, the senior general by rank; the Grand Duke Tsarevich Constantine Pavlovich; Count Rumyantsev, the Chancellor; Stein, a former Prussian minister; Armfeldt, a Swedish general; Pfuel, the chief author of the plan of campaign; Paulucci, an adjutant general and Sardinian emigre; Wolzogen — and many others. Though these men held no military position in the army, their standing gave them influence, and often a corps commander, or even the commander in chief, didn't know whether a certain question from Bennigsen, the Grand Duke, Arakcheev, or Prince Volkonsky was the questioner's own idea or the Emperor's, and whether or not a given order received in the form of advice had to be obeyed. But this was only the surface; the essential significance of the Emperor's presence and of all these people, from a courtier's perspective (and in an Emperor's vicinity all became courtiers), was clear to everyone. It was this: the Emperor did not take the title of commander in chief but controlled all the armies; the men around him were his assistants. Arakcheev was a faithful enforcer of order who served as the sovereign's bodyguard. Bennigsen was a landowner in the Vilna province who appeared to be doing the honors of the district but was actually a competent general, useful as an adviser and ready to replace Barclay. The Grand Duke was there because it suited him. The former Minister Stein was there because his advice was valuable and Emperor Alexander held him in high personal esteem. Armfeldt bitterly hated Napoleon and was a general full of self-confidence — a quality that always influenced Alexander. Paulucci was there because he was bold and decisive in speech. The adjutants general were there because they always accompanied the Emperor, and lastly and chiefly, Pfuel was there because he had drawn up the plan of campaign against Napoleon and, having persuaded Alexander to believe in its effectiveness, was directing the whole business of the war. With Pfuel was Wolzogen, who expressed Pfuel's thoughts in a more comprehensible way than Pfuel himself — who was a harsh, bookish theorist, self-confident to the point of despising everyone else — could manage.

Besides these Russians and foreigners who proposed new and unexpected ideas every day — especially the foreigners, who did so with the boldness characteristic of people working in a country not their own — there were many lesser figures accompanying the army because their principals were there.
Among the opinions and voices in this immense, restless, brilliant, and proud sphere, Prince Andrew noticed the following clearly defined factions and tendencies:

The first faction consisted of Pfuel and his followers — military theorists who believed in a science of war with immutable laws governing oblique movements, flanking maneuvers, and so forth. Pfuel and his followers demanded a retreat into the depths of the country in accordance with the precise laws of their pseudo-science of war, and they saw only barbarism, ignorance, or evil intent in every deviation from that theory. To this faction belonged the foreign nobles — Wolzogen, Wintzingerode, and others, chiefly Germans.

The second faction was the direct opposite of the first; as always, one extreme was met by representatives of the other. Its members demanded an advance from Vilna into Poland and freedom from all prearranged plans. Besides advocating bold action, this group also represented nationalism, which made them still more one-sided in the dispute. They were Russians: Bagration, Ermolov (who was beginning to come to prominence), and others. At that time a famous joke of Ermolov's was circulating: as a great favor he had supposedly petitioned the Emperor to make him a German. The men of this faction, invoking the memory of Suvorov, said that what one had to do was not theorize or stick pins in maps, but fight, beat the enemy, keep him out of Russia, and not let the army get demoralized.

The third faction — in which the Emperor had the most confidence — consisted of courtiers who tried to arrange compromises between the other two. Its members, chiefly civilians (including Arakcheev), thought and said what men who have no convictions but wish to appear to have some generally say. They said that undoubtedly war, particularly against such a genius as Bonaparte (they now called him Bonaparte), requires the most deeply considered plans and profound scientific knowledge, and in that respect Pfuel was a genius, but at the same time one had to acknowledge that theorists are often one-sided, and therefore one shouldn't rely on them absolutely but should also listen to what Pfuel's opponents and practical men experienced in warfare had to say, and then choose a middle course. They insisted on keeping the camp at Drissa, according to Pfuel's plan, but on altering the movements of the other armies. Though by this approach neither one aim nor the other could be attained, it seemed best to the members of this third faction.

The most conspicuous representative of the fourth faction was the Tsarevich, who could not forget his disillusionment at Austerlitz, where he had ridden out at the head of the Guards in his helmet and cavalry uniform as to a review, expecting to crush the French gallantly, but had unexpectedly found himself in the front line and had narrowly escaped amid the general confusion. The men of this faction had both the virtue and the defect of frankness. They feared Napoleon, recognized his strength and their own weakness, and openly said so. They said: "Nothing but sorrow, shame, and ruin will come of all this! We have abandoned Vilna and Vitebsk and shall abandon Drissa. The only sensible thing left is to make peace as soon as possible, before we are thrown out of Petersburg."
This view was widely held in the upper army circles and found support also in Petersburg and from the Chancellor, Rumyantsev, who for other reasons of state favored peace.

The fifth faction consisted of supporters of Barclay de Tolly, not so much of the man as of the minister of war and commander in chief. "Be he what he may" (they always began like that), "he is an honest, practical man and we have nobody better. Give him real power, for war cannot be waged successfully without unity of command, and he will show what he can do, as he did in Finland. If our army is well organized and strong and has retreated to Drissa without suffering any defeats, we owe this entirely to Barclay. If Barclay is now replaced by Bennigsen, all will be lost, for Bennigsen proved his incompetence as far back as 1807."

The sixth faction, the Bennigsenites, said on the contrary that there was certainly no one more active and experienced than Bennigsen: "Twist about as you may, you'll have to come to Bennigsen in the end. Let the others make mistakes now!" said they, arguing that our retreat to Drissa was a most shameful reverse and an unbroken chain of blunders. "The more mistakes that are made the better. At least it will be understood sooner that things can't go on like this. What is needed is not some Barclay or other, but a man like Bennigsen, who proved himself in 1807 and to whom Napoleon himself gave credit — a man whose authority would be willingly accepted, and Bennigsen is the only such man."

The seventh faction consisted of the sort of people who are always found around young sovereigns, and of whom there were particularly many around Alexander — generals and imperial aides-de-camp passionately devoted to the Emperor not merely as a monarch but as a man, adoring him sincerely and selflessly as Rostov had done in 1805, and who saw in him not only all the virtues but all human capabilities as well. These men, though delighted with the sovereign's refusal to command the army, nevertheless blamed him for such excessive modesty and only desired that their adored sovereign should abandon his diffidence and openly announce that he would take personal command of the army, gather a commander in chief's staff around him, and — consulting experienced theoreticians and practical men as needed — lead the troops himself, whose spirits would thereby be raised to the highest pitch.

The eighth and largest group, which outnumbered the others as ninety-nine to one, consisted of men who desired neither peace nor war, neither an advance nor a defensive camp at Drissa or anywhere else, neither Barclay nor the Emperor, neither Pfuel nor Bennigsen, but only the one most essential thing — as much advantage and pleasure for themselves as possible. In the troubled waters of conflicting and intersecting intrigues that swirled around the Emperor's headquarters, it was possible to succeed in many ways unthinkable at other times. A man who simply wanted to keep his lucrative post would today agree with Pfuel, tomorrow with his opponent, and the day after — merely to avoid responsibility or to please the Emperor — would declare that he had no opinion at all on the matter. Another who wished to gain some advantage would attract the Emperor's attention by loudly advocating the very thing the Emperor had hinted at the day before, and would argue and shout at the council, beating his chest and challenging those who disagreed to duels, thereby proving his readiness to sacrifice himself for the common good. A third, between two councils, would simply ask for a special bonus for his faithful services, well knowing that at such a moment people would be too busy to refuse. A fourth would keep arranging to appear accidentally before the Emperor's eyes. A fifth, to achieve his long-cherished aim of dining with the Emperor, would stubbornly argue for or against some newly emerging opinion and produce more or less convincing arguments to that end.

All the men of this group were fishing for decorations, promotions, and money, and in this pursuit they watched only the weathercock of imperial favor; as soon as they noticed it turning in any direction, this whole drone population of the army began blowing hard that way, making it all the harder for the Emperor to turn it elsewhere. Amid the uncertainties of the situation, with the threat of serious danger lending a peculiarly menacing character to everything, amid this vortex of intrigue, self-interest, conflicting views and feelings, and the diversity of nationalities among these people, this eighth and largest group — the people preoccupied with personal gain — introduced great confusion and obscurity into the common task. Whatever question arose, a swarm of these drones, without having finished buzzing about the previous topic, flew to the new one and by their noise drowned out and obscured the voices of those who were arguing honestly.

From among all these factions, just at the time Prince Andrew reached the army, another — a ninth — was being formed and beginning to raise its voice. This was the party of older, reasonable men experienced and capable in state affairs, who were able to take a detached view of what was happening at headquarters and to consider ways out of this muddle, indecision, confusion, and weakness.

The men of this faction said and thought that the problems stemmed mainly from the Emperor's presence in the army with his military court and the resulting indefinite, conditional, and unstable web of relationships, which was appropriate at court but harmful in an army; that a sovereign should reign but not command the army, and that the only solution was for the Emperor and his court to leave; that the mere presence of the Emperor paralyzed fifty thousand men needed to guarantee his personal safety; and that the worst commander in chief acting independently would be better than the best one hampered by the presence and authority of the monarch.

Just at the time Prince Andrew was living idly at Drissa, Shishkov, the Secretary of State and one of the chief representatives of this faction, wrote a letter to the Emperor which Arakcheev and Balashev agreed to sign. In this letter, taking advantage of the permission given him by the Emperor to discuss the general course of affairs, he respectfully suggested — on the grounds that it was necessary for the sovereign to rouse the people of the capital to a warlike spirit — that the Emperor should leave the army.

This stirring of the people by their sovereign and his call to them to defend their country — the very move that was the chief cause of Russia's triumph, insofar as it was produced by the Tsar's personal presence in Moscow — was suggested to the Emperor and accepted by him as a pretext for leaving the army.

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: This letter had not yet been presented to the Emperor when Barclay, one day at dinner, informed Bolkonsky that the sovereign wished to see him personally, to question him about Turkey, and that Prince Andrew was to present himself at Bennigsen's quarters at six that evening.

News was received at the Emperor's quarters that very day of a fresh movement by Napoleon which might endanger the army — news that later proved to be false. And that morning Colonel Michaud had ridden around the Drissa fortifications with the Emperor and had pointed out to him that this fortified camp, constructed by Pfuel and until then considered a masterpiece of tactical science that would ensure Napoleon's destruction, was in fact an absurdity threatening the destruction of the Russian army.

Prince Andrew arrived at Bennigsen's quarters — a moderate-sized country gentleman's house situated on the very banks of the river. Neither Bennigsen nor the Emperor was there, but Chernyshev, the Emperor's aide-de-camp, received Bolkonsky and told him that the Emperor, accompanied by General Bennigsen and Marquis Paulucci, had gone out a second time that day to inspect the Drissa fortifications, about whose suitability serious doubts were beginning to arise.

Chernyshev was sitting at a window in the first room with a French novel in his hand. This room had probably been a music room; there was still an organ in it on which some rugs were piled, and in one corner stood the folding bed of Bennigsen's adjutant. This adjutant was also there, sitting dozing on the rolled-up bedding, clearly exhausted by work or by socializing. Two doors led from the room: one straight into what had been the drawing room, and another on the right to the study. Through the first door came the sound of voices conversing in German and occasionally in French. In that drawing room, by the Emperor's wish, there was assembled — not a formal military council (the Emperor preferred vagueness) — but a group of people whose opinions he wished to hear given the looming difficulties. It was not a war council but rather an informal advisory session for the Emperor personally. To this semi-council had been invited the Swedish General Armfeldt, Adjutant General Wolzogen, Wintzingerode (whom Napoleon had called a renegade French subject), Michaud, Toll, Count Stein — who was not a military man at all — and Pfuel himself, who, as Prince Andrew had heard, was the driving force behind everything. Prince Andrew had an opportunity to get a good look at Pfuel, who arrived soon after him and passed through to the drawing room, pausing briefly to speak to Chernyshev.

At first sight, Pfuel — in his poorly fitted Russian general's uniform, which looked on him like a costume — seemed familiar to Prince Andrew, though he was seeing him for the first time. There was something of Weyrother, Mack, and Schmidt about him, and many other German theorist-generals Prince Andrew had seen in 1805, but he was more typical than any of them. Prince Andrew had never yet seen a German theorist who combined all those characteristics to such a degree.

Pfuel was short and very thin but broad-boned, of coarse, sturdy build, broad in the hips and with prominent shoulder blades. His face was much wrinkled and his eyes deep-set. His hair had evidently been hastily smoothed down in front at the temples but stuck up behind in comical little tufts. He entered the room, looking around restlessly and irritably, as if afraid of everything in that large space. Awkwardly holding up his sword, he addressed Chernyshev and asked in German where the Emperor was. Clearly he wanted to get through the rooms as quickly as possible, finish with the bows and greetings, and sit down to work in front of a map, where he would feel at home. He nodded hurriedly in reply to Chernyshev and smiled sarcastically on hearing that the sovereign was inspecting the fortifications that he, Pfuel, had designed according to his theory. He muttered something to himself in a bass voice, as self-assured Germans do — it might have been "stupid fellow" or "the whole affair will be ruined" or "something absurd will come of it." Prince Andrew didn't catch what he said and would have passed on, but Chernyshev introduced him to Pfuel, mentioning that Prince Andrew had just returned from Turkey, where the war had ended so successfully. Pfuel barely glanced — not so much at Prince Andrew as past him — and said with a laugh: "That must have been a fine tactical war"; and, laughing contemptuously, went into the room from which the voices were coming.

Pfuel, always inclined to be irritably sarcastic, was particularly upset that day, evidently because they had dared to inspect and criticize his camp in his absence. From this brief encounter with Pfuel, Prince Andrew — thanks to his Austerlitz experiences — was able to form a clear picture of the man. Pfuel was one of those hopelessly and immutably self-confident men, self-confident to the point of martyrdom as only Germans are, because only Germans base their self-confidence on an abstract notion — science, that is, the supposed knowledge of absolute truth. A Frenchman is self-assured because he regards himself personally, both in mind and body, as irresistibly attractive to men and women. An Englishman is self-assured because he is a citizen of the best-organized state in the world, and therefore as an Englishman always knows what to do and knows that whatever he does as an Englishman is undoubtedly correct. An Italian is self-assured because he is excitable and easily forgets himself and other people. A Russian is self-assured precisely because he knows nothing and does not want to know anything, since he doesn't believe that anything can truly be known. The German's self-assurance is the worst of all — stronger and more repulsive than any other — because he imagines that he knows the truth, that is, science, which he himself has invented but which is for him the absolute truth.

Pfuel was clearly of that sort. He had a science — the theory of oblique movements derived from the history of Frederick the Great's wars — and everything he encountered in more recent warfare seemed to him absurd and barbarous: monstrous collisions in which so many blunders were committed by both sides that these wars could not be called wars at all — they didn't conform to the theory and therefore could not serve as material for science.

In 1806 Pfuel had been one of those responsible for the plan of campaign that ended in Jena and Auerstadt, but he saw not the slightest proof of the fallibility of his theory in the disasters of that war. On the contrary, the deviations from his theory were, in his view, the sole cause of the entire catastrophe, and with characteristically gleeful sarcasm he would say: "There, I said the whole affair would go to the devil!" Pfuel was one of those theorists who so love their theory that they lose sight of its object — its practical application. His love of theory made him hate everything practical, and he would not listen to it. He was even pleased by failures, because failures resulting from deviations from theory only proved to him the accuracy of his theory.

He said a few words to Prince Andrew and Chernyshev about the current war, with the air of a man who knows beforehand that everything will go wrong and who is not displeased that it should be so. The unbrushed tufts of hair sticking up behind and the hastily smoothed hair at his temples expressed this most eloquently.
He passed into the next room, and the deep, querulous sounds of his voice were immediately heard from there.

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: Prince Andrew's eyes were still following Pfuel out of the room when Count Bennigsen entered hurriedly, and nodding to Bolkonsky but not pausing, went into the study, giving instructions to his adjutant as he went. The Emperor was following him, and Bennigsen had hurried ahead to make some preparations and be ready to receive the sovereign. Chernyshev and Prince Andrew went out onto the porch, where the Emperor, who looked fatigued, was dismounting. Marquis Paulucci was talking to him with particular intensity, and the Emperor, with his head tilted to the left, was listening with a displeased expression. The Emperor moved forward, clearly wanting to end the conversation, but the flushed and excited Italian, ignoring etiquette, followed him and kept talking.

"And as for the man who advised building this camp — the Drissa camp," said Paulucci, as the Emperor mounted the steps and noticed Prince Andrew's unfamiliar face, "as to that person, sire..." continued Paulucci desperately, apparently unable to stop himself, "the man who advised the Drissa camp — I see no alternative but the madhouse or the gallows!"
Without paying attention to the end of the Italian's remarks, and as though not hearing them, the Emperor recognized Bolkonsky and addressed him warmly.
"I'm very glad to see you! Go in where they are meeting, and wait for me."

The Emperor went into the study. He was followed by Prince Peter Mikhaylovich Volkonsky and Baron Stein, and the door closed behind them. Prince Andrew, taking advantage of the Emperor's permission, accompanied Paulucci — whom he had known in Turkey — into the drawing room where the council was assembled.

Prince Peter Mikhaylovich Volkonsky occupied the position of, as it were, chief of the Emperor's staff. He came out of the study into the drawing room with some maps which he spread on a table, and put questions on which he wished to hear the opinions of those present. What had happened was that news (which later proved false) had been received during the night of a French movement to outflank the Drissa camp.

The first to speak was General Armfeldt, who to address the difficulty unexpectedly proposed an entirely new position away from the Petersburg and Moscow roads. The reason for this was inexplicable (unless he wanted to show that he too could have an opinion), but he urged that the army should unite at this point and there await the enemy. It was clear that Armfeldt had thought out this plan long ago and now presented it not so much to answer the questions posed — which in fact his plan did not answer — but to seize the opportunity to air it. It was one of the millions of proposals, one as good as another, that could be made as long as it was completely unknown what form the war would take. Some disputed his arguments, others supported them. Young Count Toll objected to the Swedish general's views more heatedly than anyone else, and in the course of the argument drew from his pocket a well-filled notebook, which he asked permission to read. In these voluminous notes Toll suggested an entirely different scheme from either Armfeldt's or Pfuel's plan. In response to Toll, Paulucci proposed an advance and an attack, which he said was the only way to escape the present uncertainty and the trap (as he called the Drissa camp) in which they were stuck.

Throughout all these discussions, Pfuel and his interpreter Wolzogen (his "bridge" in court relations) remained silent. Pfuel merely snorted contemptuously and turned away, making it clear he would never lower himself to respond to the nonsense he was hearing. So when Prince Volkonsky, who was chairing the meeting, called on him for his opinion, he simply said:

"Why ask me? General Armfeldt has proposed a splendid position with an exposed rear, or why not this Italian gentleman's plan of attack — very fine! Or a retreat — also good! Why ask me?" he said. "After all, you yourselves know everything better than I do."
But when Volkonsky said with a frown that he was asking in the Emperor's name, Pfuel rose and, suddenly animated, began to speak:

"Everything has been ruined, everything muddled! Everyone thought they knew better than I did, and now you come to me! How can it be fixed? There is nothing to fix! The principles I laid down must be followed strictly," he said, drumming on the table with his bony fingers. "What is the difficulty? Nonsense! Childishness!"

He strode to the map and, speaking rapidly, began demonstrating that no eventuality could undermine the effectiveness of the Drissa camp, that everything had been foreseen, and that if the enemy were truly going to outflank it, they would inevitably be destroyed.

Paulucci, who did not know German, began questioning him in French. Wolzogen came to his chief's aid — Pfuel spoke French badly — and began translating for him, barely able to keep pace as Pfuel rapidly demonstrated that not only everything that had happened, but everything that could possibly happen, had been foreseen in his plan, and that if difficulties had arisen, the entire fault lay in the fact that his plan had not been executed precisely. He laughed sarcastically, he proved his points, and finally ceased his demonstration with contempt, like a mathematician who stops bothering to prove a problem he considers already proven. Wolzogen took over and continued explaining in French, turning every now and then to Pfuel: "Is that not so, Your Excellency?" But Pfuel, like a man in a fight who lashes out at his own allies, shouted angrily at his own supporter Wolzogen:
"Well, of course — what more is there to explain?"
Paulucci and Michaud attacked Wolzogen simultaneously in French. Armfeldt addressed Pfuel in German. Toll explained things to Volkonsky in Russian. Prince Andrew listened and observed in silence.

Of all these men, Prince Andrew felt the most sympathy for Pfuel — angry, determined, and absurdly self-confident though he was. Of everyone present, he alone was clearly not seeking anything for himself, harbored no hatred toward anyone, and simply wanted the plan he had developed through years of work to be carried out. He was ridiculous and unpleasantly sarcastic, yet he inspired involuntary respect through his boundless devotion to an idea. Besides this, the remarks of all the others except Pfuel shared one trait that had not been noticeable at the council of war in 1805: there was now a barely concealed panic fear of Napoleon's genius, evident in every rejoinder. Everything was assumed to be possible for Napoleon; they expected him from every direction and invoked his terrible name to demolish each other's proposals. Pfuel alone seemed to regard Napoleon as a barbarian, no different from anyone else who opposed his theory. But beyond respect, Pfuel also stirred pity in Prince Andrew. From the tone in which the courtiers addressed him, from the way Paulucci had spoken of him to the Emperor, and above all from a certain desperation in Pfuel's own manner, it was clear that the others knew — and Pfuel himself sensed — that his downfall was at hand. And despite his self-assurance and his gruff German sarcasm, he was pitiable, with his hair neatly smoothed at the temples and sticking up in tufts at the back. Though he hid it behind a show of irritation and contempt, he was plainly in despair that the sole remaining chance to test his theory through a great experiment and prove its soundness to the whole world was slipping away from him.

The discussions dragged on, and the longer they lasted, the more heated the disputes became — culminating in shouts and personal attacks — and the less possible it was to reach any general conclusion. Prince Andrew, listening to this babel of languages and to these conjectures, plans, refutations, and outbursts, felt nothing but amazement at what they were all saying. A thought that had long since and often occurred to him during his military service — the idea that there is not and cannot be any science of war, and that therefore there can be no such thing as military genius — now struck him as an obvious truth. "What theory and science can apply to a matter whose conditions and circumstances are unknown and cannot be defined, especially when the strength of the forces involved cannot be measured? No one was or is able to foresee what position our army or the enemy's will be in tomorrow, and no one can gauge the real strength of any given detachment. Sometimes — when there is no coward at the front to shout 'We're cut off!' and start running, but instead a brave and cheerful fellow who shouts 'Hurrah!' — a force of five thousand is worth thirty thousand, as at Schön Grabern, while at other times fifty thousand flee from eight thousand, as at Austerlitz. What science can govern a matter in which, as in all practical affairs, nothing can be precisely determined and everything depends on countless conditions whose significance reveals itself only at a particular moment that no one can predict? Armfeldt says our army is cut in half, and Paulucci says we have the French between two fires; Michaud says the Drissa camp is worthless because the river is behind it, while Pfuel says that is exactly what makes it strong; Toll proposes one plan, Armfeldt another — and they are all good and all bad, because the merits of any proposal can only be seen at the moment of execution. And why do they all talk of 'military genius'? Is a man a genius because he can order bread to be brought up at the right time and tell soldiers to go right or left? It is only because military leaders are surrounded by pomp, power, and crowds of sycophants who flatter authority by attributing to it qualities of genius it does not possess. The best generals I have known were, on the contrary, stupid or absent-minded men. Bagration was the best — Napoleon himself admitted it. And Napoleon himself! I remember his smug, self-satisfied face on the field of Austerlitz. Not only does a good commander not need any special qualities — on the contrary, he needs the absence of the highest and best human attributes: love, poetry, tenderness, and philosophic, questioning doubt. He should be narrow-minded, firmly convinced that what he is doing is enormously important (otherwise he will lack the necessary patience), and only then will he be a brave leader. God forbid that he should be humane, that he should love or feel pity, or think about what is just and unjust. It is no wonder that a theory of their 'genius' was invented for them long ago, because they hold power! The success of a military action depends not on them but on the man in the ranks who shouts 'We're lost!' or who shouts 'Hurrah!' And only in the ranks can one serve with the assurance of being truly useful."
So thought Prince Andrew as he listened to the debate, and he roused himself only when Paulucci called to him and everyone began to leave.

At the review the next day, the Emperor asked Prince Andrew where he would like to serve, and Prince Andrew lost his standing in court circles forever by not asking to remain attached to the sovereign's person, but requesting permission to serve with the army.

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Before the start of the campaign, Rostov had received a letter from his parents in which they told him briefly of Natasha's illness and the breaking off of her engagement to Prince Andrew (which they explained by saying that Natasha had rejected him), and again asked Nicholas to retire from the army and return home. On receiving this letter, Nicholas didn't even try to get leave or to retire, but wrote to his parents that he was sorry Natasha was ill and her engagement broken off, and that he would do all he could to meet their wishes. To Sonya he wrote separately.

"Adored friend of my soul!" he wrote. "Nothing but honor could keep me from returning to the country. But now, at the start of the campaign, I would feel dishonored — not only in my comrades' eyes but in my own — if I preferred my own happiness to my love and duty to the Fatherland. But this shall be our last separation. Believe me, as soon as the war is over, if I am still alive and still loved by you, I will throw up everything and fly to you, to press you forever to my loving heart."

It was in fact only the start of the campaign that prevented Rostov from returning home as he had promised and marrying Sonya. The autumn in Otradnoe with the hunting, and the winter with the Christmas holidays and Sonya's love, had opened up to him a vision of tranquil rural joys and peace such as he had never known before, and which now beckoned to him. "A wonderful wife, children, a good pack of hounds, a dozen leashes of swift borzois, farming, neighbors, elected public service..." he thought. But now the campaign was beginning, and he had to stay with his regiment. And since it had to be so, Nicholas Rostov, as was natural to him, found contentment in the life he led in the regiment and managed to find pleasure in it.

On his return from his leave, Nicholas was joyfully welcomed by his comrades and sent to buy remount horses. He brought back from Ukraine excellent horses that pleased him and earned him praise from his commanders. During his absence he had been promoted to captain, and when the regiment was put on a war footing with increased numbers, he was again given command of his old squadron.

The campaign began, the regiment was moved into Poland on double pay, new officers arrived, new men and horses, and above all everybody was infected with the merrily excited mood that goes with the start of a war. Rostov, conscious of his good standing in the regiment, devoted himself entirely to the pleasures and interests of military service, though he knew that sooner or later he would have to give them up.

The troops retreated from Vilna for various complicated reasons of state, political and strategic. Each step of the retreat was accompanied by a complex interplay of interests, arguments, and passions at headquarters. For the Pavlograd hussars, however, the whole retreat during the finest period of summer, with adequate supplies, was a very simple and pleasant affair.

It was only at headquarters that there was depression, uneasiness, and intrigue; in the body of the army no one asked where they were going or why. If they were sorry to retreat, it was only because they had to leave billets they had grown used to, or some pretty young Polish lady. If the thought that things looked bad happened to enter anyone's head, he tried to be as cheerful as befits a good soldier and not to think about the big picture, but only about the task nearest at hand. First they camped cheerfully near Vilna, making friends with the Polish landowners, preparing for reviews, and being reviewed by the Emperor and other high commanders. Then came an order to retreat to Sventsiany and destroy any supplies they couldn't carry. Sventsiany was remembered by the hussars only as "the drunken camp" — a name the whole army gave to their time there — because many complaints were made against the troops, who, using the order to collect supplies as cover, also took horses, carriages, and carpets from the Polish landowners. Rostov remembered Sventsiany because on the first day of their arrival in that small town he had to replace his sergeant major and was unable to manage all the drunken men of his squadron, who had secretly appropriated five barrels of old beer. From Sventsiany they retreated farther and farther to Drissa, and then beyond Drissa, drawing close to the Russian heartland.
On July thirteenth the Pavlograds took part in a serious engagement for the first time.
On the twelfth of July, the eve of that action, there was a violent storm of rain and hail. In general, the summer of 1812 was remarkable for its storms.

The two Pavlograd squadrons were camped in a field of rye, already in ear but completely trampled by cattle and horses. The rain was falling in torrents, and Rostov with a young officer named Ilyin, his protege, was sitting in a hastily built shelter. An officer of their regiment, with long mustaches extending onto his cheeks, who after riding to the staff had been caught by the rain, came into Rostov's shelter.
"I've come from the staff, Count. Have you heard about Raevsky's exploit?"
And the officer gave them details of the Saltanov battle, which he had heard at the staff.

Rostov, smoking his pipe and turning his head as the water trickled down his neck, listened with half an ear, with an occasional glance at Ilyin, who was pressing close beside him. This officer, a boy of sixteen who had recently joined the regiment, now stood in the same relation to Nicholas that Nicholas had been to Denisov seven years before. Ilyin tried to imitate Rostov in everything and adored him as a girl might have done.

Zdrzhinski, the officer with the long mustaches, spoke grandly of the Saltanov dam being "a Russian Thermopylae" and of how a deed worthy of antiquity had been performed by General Raevsky. He described how Raevsky had led his two sons onto the dam under terrific fire and had charged with them beside him. Rostov heard the story and not only said nothing to encourage Zdrzhinski's enthusiasm but, on the contrary, looked like a man ashamed of what he was hearing, though with no intention of contradicting it. Since the campaigns of Austerlitz and 1807, Rostov knew from experience that men always lie when describing military exploits, as he himself had done when telling them; besides, he had enough experience to know that nothing in war happens the way we can imagine or describe it. And so he didn't like Zdrzhinski's tale, nor did he like Zdrzhinski himself, who with his mustaches extending over his cheeks, leaned low over his listener's face as was his habit, crowding Rostov in the cramped shelter. Rostov looked at him in silence. "In the first place, there must have been such confusion and crowding on the dam being attacked that if Raevsky did lead his sons there, it could only have affected about a dozen men nearest to him," he thought. "The rest couldn't have seen who came onto the dam with Raevsky. And even those who did see wouldn't have been much inspired, because what did they care about Raevsky's tender paternal feelings when their own lives were at stake? And besides, the fate of the Fatherland didn't depend on whether they took the Saltanov dam or not, as we're told was the case at Thermopylae. So why would he have made such a sacrifice? And why bring his own children into battle? I wouldn't have brought my brother Petya there, or even Ilyin, who's a stranger to me but a nice lad — I would have tried to put them somewhere under cover," Nicholas continued to think as he listened to Zdrzhinski. But he didn't express his thoughts, for in such matters too he had learned from experience. He knew that this tale redounded to the glory of the Russian army and so one had to pretend not to doubt it. And he acted accordingly.

"I can't stand this any more," said Ilyin, noticing that Rostov didn't enjoy Zdrzhinski's conversation. "My stockings and shirt... and the water's running into my seat! I'll go look for shelter. The rain seems lighter."
Ilyin went out and Zdrzhinski rode away.
Five minutes later Ilyin, splashing through the mud, came running back to the shelter.
"Hurrah! Rostov, come quick! I've found it! About two hundred yards away there's a tavern where our fellows have already gathered. We can at least get dry there, and Mary Hendrikhovna's there."

Mary Hendrikhovna was the wife of the regimental doctor, a pretty young German woman he had married in Poland. The doctor, whether from lack of means or because he didn't like to be separated from his young wife in the early days of their marriage, took her along with him wherever the hussar regiment went, and his jealousy had become a standing joke among the hussar officers.

Rostov threw his cloak over his shoulders, shouted to Lavrushka to follow with the things, and — now slipping in the mud, now splashing right through it — set off with Ilyin in the lessening rain and the darkness that was occasionally torn by distant lightning.
"Rostov, where are you?"
"Here. What lightning!" they called to one another.

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: In the tavern, in front of which stood the doctor's covered cart, there were already about five officers. Mary Hendrikhovna, a plump little blonde German in a dressing jacket and nightcap, was sitting on a broad bench in the front corner. Her husband, the doctor, lay asleep behind her. Rostov and Ilyin, on entering the room, were greeted with merry shouts and laughter.
"My, how jolly we are!" said Rostov, laughing.
"And why are you standing there gaping?"
"What dandies they are! Look, the water's streaming off them! Don't get our drawing room so wet."
"Don't mess up Mary Hendrikhovna's dress!" cried other voices.

Rostov and Ilyin hurried to find a corner where they could change into dry clothes without embarrassing Mary Hendrikhovna. They were heading into a tiny alcove behind a partition, but found it completely occupied by three officers playing cards by the light of a single candle on an empty box, and these officers absolutely refused to give up their spot. Mary Hendrikhovna lent them a petticoat to use as a curtain, and behind that screen Rostov and Ilyin, with Lavrushka's help — he had brought their kits — changed out of their wet things into dry ones.

A fire was built up in the broken brick stove. A board was found, set on two saddles and covered with a horse blanket, a small samovar was produced along with a flask and half a bottle of rum, and having asked Mary Hendrikhovna to preside, they all crowded around her. One offered her a clean handkerchief to wipe her charming hands, another spread a jacket under her small feet to keep them from the damp, another draped his coat over the window to block the draft, and yet another waved flies away from her husband's face so he wouldn't wake up.
"Leave him alone," said Mary Hendrikhovna, smiling timidly and happily. "He's sleeping well as it is, after a sleepless night."
"Oh no, Mary Hendrikhovna," replied the officer, "one must look after the doctor. Perhaps he'll take pity on me someday, when it comes to cutting off a leg or an arm."

There were only three tumblers, the water was so muddy that you couldn't tell whether the tea was strong or weak, and the samovar held only six cups of water, but this made it all the more pleasant to take turns, in order of seniority, receiving one's cup from Mary Hendrikhovna's plump little hands with their short, not perfectly clean nails. All the officers appeared to be, and really were, in love with her that evening. Even those playing cards behind the partition soon abandoned their game and came over to the samovar, yielding to the general mood of courting Mary Hendrikhovna. She, seeing herself surrounded by such brilliant and polite young men, beamed with satisfaction — try as she might to hide it — and was clearly flustered each time her husband stirred in his sleep behind her.

There was only one spoon; sugar was more plentiful than anything else, but it took too long to dissolve, so it was decided that Mary Hendrikhovna should stir the sugar for everyone in turn. Rostov received his tumbler, and adding some rum to it, asked Mary Hendrikhovna to stir it.
"But you take it without sugar?" she said, smiling all the time, as if everything she said and everything the others said was very funny and had a double meaning.
"It's not the sugar I want — only that your little hand should stir my tea."
Mary Hendrikhovna agreed and began looking for the spoon, which someone had meanwhile snatched up.
"Use your finger, Mary Hendrikhovna — it will be even nicer," said Rostov.
"Too hot!" she replied, blushing with pleasure.
Ilyin put a few drops of rum into the bucket of water and brought it to Mary Hendrikhovna, asking her to stir it with her finger.
"This is my cup," said he. "Just dip your finger in and I'll drink it all up."

When they had emptied the samovar, Rostov took a pack of cards and proposed they play "Kings" with Mary Hendrikhovna. They drew lots to decide who would be on her team. At Rostov's suggestion, it was agreed that whoever became "King" should have the right to kiss Mary Hendrikhovna's hand, and that the "Fool" should go refill and reheat the samovar for the doctor when he woke up.
"Well, but what if Mary Hendrikhovna is 'King'?" asked Ilyin.
"As it is, she's Queen — and her word is law!"

They had hardly begun playing when the doctor's tousled head suddenly appeared from behind Mary Hendrikhovna. He had been awake for some time, listening to what was being said, and evidently found nothing entertaining or amusing in what was going on. His face was sad and gloomy. Without greeting the officers, he scratched himself and asked to be allowed to pass, as they were blocking the way. As soon as he left the room, all the officers burst into loud laughter and Mary Hendrikhovna blushed till her eyes filled with tears — thereby becoming still more attractive to them. Returning from the yard, the doctor told his wife (who had stopped smiling so happily and looked at him with alarm, waiting for the verdict) that the rain had stopped and they must go sleep in their covered cart, or everything in it would be stolen.
"But I'll send an orderly... Two of them!" said Rostov. "What an idea, doctor!"
"I'll stand guard on it myself!" said Ilyin.
"No, gentlemen, you've had your sleep, but I haven't slept for two nights," replied the doctor, and he sat down gloomily beside his wife, waiting for the game to end.

Seeing his gloomy face as he frowned at his wife, the officers grew still merrier, and some of them couldn't suppress laughter for which they hastily sought plausible pretexts. When he had gone, taking his wife with him, and had settled in their covered cart, the officers lay down in the tavern, covering themselves with their wet cloaks, but couldn't sleep for a long time; now they exchanged remarks, recalling the doctor's uneasiness and his wife's delight, now they ran out to the porch and reported what was happening in the covered cart. Several times Rostov, pulling his cloak over his head, tried to sleep, but some remark would rouse him and conversation would be resumed, accompanied by unreasoning, merry, childlike laughter.

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: It was nearly three o'clock but no one was yet asleep when the quartermaster appeared with orders to move on to the little town of Ostrovna. Still laughing and talking, the officers began hurriedly getting ready and again boiled some muddy water in the samovar. But Rostov went off to his squadron without waiting for tea. Day was breaking, the rain had stopped, and the clouds were dispersing. It felt damp and cold, especially in clothes still wet. As they left the tavern in the twilight of dawn, Rostov and Ilyin both glanced under the wet and glistening leather hood of the doctor's cart, from beneath which his feet were sticking out, and in the middle of which his wife's nightcap was visible and her sleepy breathing audible.
"She really is a dear little thing," said Rostov to Ilyin, who was following him.
"A charming woman!" said Ilyin, with all the gravity of a boy of sixteen.

Half an hour later the squadron was lined up on the road. The command was heard to "mount" and the soldiers crossed themselves and mounted. Rostov, riding in front, gave the order "Forward!" and the hussars, with clanking sabers and quiet talk, their horses' hoofs splashing in the mud, moved out in fours along the broad road lined with birch trees on each side, following the infantry and a battery that had gone ahead.

Tattered, blue-purple clouds, reddening in the east, were scudding before the wind. It was growing lighter and lighter. That curly grass which always grows along country roadsides became clearly visible, still wet from the night's rain; the drooping branches of the birches, also wet, swayed in the wind and flung down bright drops of water to one side. The soldiers' faces grew more and more visible. Rostov, always closely followed by Ilyin, rode along the side of the road between two rows of birch trees.

When campaigning, Rostov allowed himself the luxury of riding not a regimental but a Cossack horse. As a judge of horses and a sportsman, he had lately acquired a large, fine, spirited Don horse, dun-colored with a light mane and tail, and when he rode it no one could outrun him. To ride this horse was a pleasure, and he thought of the horse, of the morning, of the doctor's wife, but not once of the approaching danger.

Formerly, when going into action, Rostov had felt afraid; now he had not the slightest feeling of fear. He was fearless not because he had gotten used to being under fire (one cannot get used to danger), but because he had learned how to manage his thoughts when in danger. He had trained himself, when going into action, to think about anything except what would seem most likely to interest him — the approaching danger. During the first period of his service, hard as he tried and much as he reproached himself for cowardice, he had been unable to do this, but with time it came naturally. Now he rode beside Ilyin under the birch trees, occasionally plucking leaves from a branch that met his hand, sometimes touching his horse's flank with his foot, or without turning around handing a finished pipe to a hussar riding behind him, all with as calm and carefree an air as though he were merely out for a ride. He glanced with pity at the anxious face of Ilyin, who talked much and in great agitation. He knew from experience the torment of terror and anticipation of death the young officer was going through, and knew that only time could help him.

As soon as the sun appeared in a clear strip of sky beneath the clouds, the wind died down, as if it dared not spoil the beauty of the summer morning after the storm; drops still fell, but straight down now, and all was still. The full sun appeared on the horizon and disappeared behind a long narrow cloud above it. A few minutes later it reappeared, brighter still, from behind the top of the cloud, tearing its edge. Everything grew bright and glittered. And with that light, and as if in answer to it, came the sound of guns ahead of them.
Before Rostov had time to consider and estimate the distance of that firing, Count Ostermann-Tolstoy's adjutant came galloping from Vitebsk with orders to advance at a trot along the road.

The squadron overtook and passed the infantry and the battery — which had also quickened their pace — rode down a hill, and passing through an empty and deserted village ascended again. The horses began to lather and the men to flush.
"Halt! Dress your ranks!" the regimental commander was heard ahead. "Forward by the left. Walk, march!" came the command.

And the hussars, passing along the line of troops on the left flank of the Russian position, halted behind the Uhlans who were in the front line. To the right stood the Russian infantry in a dense column — the reserve. Higher up the hill, on the very skyline, the Russian guns were visible through the wonderfully clear air, brightly lit by slanting morning sunbeams. In front, beyond a hollow dale, the enemy's columns and guns could be seen. The Russian advance line, already in action, could be heard briskly exchanging fire with the enemy in the dale.

At these sounds, long unheard, Rostov's spirits rose, as at the strains of the most stirring music. Tap-tap-tap! the shots cracked, now together, now several quickly one after another. Again all was silent, and then again it sounded as if someone were walking on firecrackers and setting them off.

The hussars remained in the same place for about an hour. A cannonade began. Count Ostermann with his suite rode up behind the squadron, stopped, spoke to the regiment's commander, and rode up the hill to the guns.
After Ostermann had gone, a command rang out to the Uhlans.
"Form column! Prepare to charge!"

The infantry in front of them split into platoons to let the cavalry pass. The Uhlans started, the streamers on their lances fluttering, and trotted downhill toward the French cavalry visible below to the left.

As soon as the Uhlans descended the hill, the hussars were ordered up it to support the battery. As they took the positions vacated by the Uhlans, bullets came from the front, whining and whistling, but fell spent without doing any damage.

The sounds, which he had not heard for so long, had an even more pleasurable and exhilarating effect on Rostov than the earlier firing. Drawing himself up, he surveyed the battlefield opening out before him from the hill, and with his whole soul followed the movement of the Uhlans. They swooped down close to the French dragoons; something confused happened there amid the smoke, and five minutes later the Uhlans were galloping back — not to the place they had left but more to the left, and among the orange-colored Uhlans on chestnut horses, and behind them in a large group, blue French dragoons on gray horses could be seen.

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: Rostov, with his keen sportsman's eye, was one of the first to spot the blue French dragoons chasing the Russian Uhlans. Nearer and nearer, in disorderly crowds, came the Uhlans and the French dragoons pursuing them. He could already see how these men, who looked so small at the foot of the hill, were jostling and overtaking one another, waving their arms and sabers in the air.

Rostov watched what was happening before him as if at a hunt. He felt instinctively that if the hussars struck at the French dragoons now, the dragoons couldn't withstand them, but the charge had to happen immediately — at that very moment — or it would be too late. He looked around. A captain standing beside him was staring like himself with eyes fixed on the cavalry below.
"Andrew Sevastyanych!" said Rostov. "You know, we could crush them..."
"A fine thing too!" replied the captain, "and really..."

Rostov, without waiting to hear him out, spurred his horse, galloped to the front of his squadron, and before he had time to finish giving the word of command, the whole squadron, sharing his instinct, was following him. Rostov himself didn't know how or why he did it. He acted as he did when hunting — without reflecting or thinking. He saw the dragoons near and disordered; he knew they couldn't withstand an attack — knew there was only this one moment, and that if he let it pass it wouldn't return. The bullets were whining and whistling so stimulatingly around him and his horse was so eager to go that he couldn't hold back. He spurred his horse, gave the word of command, and immediately, hearing behind him the thundering hooves of his deployed squadron, rode at full trot downhill toward the dragoons. Hardly had they reached the bottom of the hill before their pace instinctively changed to a gallop, which grew faster and faster as they drew nearer to the Uhlans and the French dragoons galloping after them. The dragoons were now close at hand. On seeing the hussars, those in front began to turn while those behind started to pull up. With the same feeling with which he had galloped to cut off a wolf, Rostov gave full rein to his Don horse and galloped to intersect the path of the dragoons' disordered lines. One Uhlan stopped, another who was on foot flung himself to the ground to avoid being knocked over, and a riderless horse fell in among the hussars. Nearly all the French dragoons were galloping back. Rostov, picking out one on a gray horse, dashed after him. On the way he came to a bush; his gallant horse cleared it, and almost before he had righted himself in the saddle he saw that he would immediately overtake the enemy he had singled out. That Frenchman, by his uniform an officer, was going at a gallop, crouching on his gray horse and urging it on with his saber. In another instant Rostov's horse dashed its chest against the hindquarters of the officer's horse, almost knocking it over, and at the same instant Rostov, without knowing why, raised his saber and struck the Frenchman with it.

The instant he had done this, all Rostov's excitement vanished. The officer fell — not so much from the blow, which had only slightly cut his arm above the elbow, as from the shock to his horse and from fright. Rostov reined in his horse and his eyes sought his foe to see whom he had conquered. The French dragoon officer was hopping with one foot on the ground, the other caught in the stirrup. His eyes, screwed up with fear as if he expected another blow at any moment, gazed up at Rostov with shrinking terror. His pale and mud-stained face — fair and young, with a dimple in the chin and light blue eyes — was not an enemy's face at all suited to a battlefield, but a perfectly ordinary, domestic face. Before Rostov had decided what to do with him, the officer cried: "I surrender!" He hurriedly but vainly tried to free his foot from the stirrup and didn't take his frightened blue eyes from Rostov's face. Some hussars who galloped up freed his foot and helped him into the saddle. On all sides the hussars were busy with the dragoons; one was wounded, but though his face was bleeding he wouldn't give up his horse; another was perched behind a hussar with his arms around him; a third was being helped by a hussar to mount. In front, the French infantry were firing as they ran. The hussars galloped hastily back with their prisoners. Rostov galloped back with the rest, aware of an unpleasant feeling of heaviness in his heart. Something vague and confused, which he couldn't account for at all, had come over him with the capture of that officer and the blow he had dealt him.

Count Ostermann-Tolstoy met the returning hussars, sent for Rostov, thanked him, and said he would report his gallant deed to the Emperor and would recommend him for the St. George's Cross. When sent for by Count Ostermann, Rostov, remembering that he had charged without orders, felt sure his commander was summoning him to punish him for breach of discipline. Ostermann's flattering words and promise of a reward should therefore have pleased him all the more, but he still felt that same vaguely disagreeable sense of moral unease. "But what on earth is bothering me?" he asked himself as he rode back from the general. "Ilyin? No, he's safe. Have I disgraced myself in some way? No, that's not it." Something else, resembling remorse, tormented him. "Yes, oh yes — that French officer with the dimple. And I remember how my arm hesitated when I raised it."

Rostov saw the prisoners being led away and galloped after them to get another look at his Frenchman with the dimple on his chin. He was sitting in his foreign uniform on a hussar packhorse and looked anxiously around. The sword cut on his arm could hardly be called a wound. He glanced at Rostov with a forced smile and waved his hand in greeting. Rostov still felt the same indefinite sense of shame.

All that day and the next his friends and comrades noticed that Rostov, without being sulky or angry, was silent, thoughtful, and preoccupied. He drank reluctantly, tried to be alone, and kept turning something over in his mind.

Rostov was constantly thinking about that brilliant exploit of his, which to his amazement had earned him the St. George's Cross and even given him a reputation for bravery, and there was something he couldn't understand at all. "So others are even more afraid than I am!" he thought. "So that's all there is to what they call heroism! And did I do it for my country's sake? And how was he to blame, with his dimple and blue eyes? And how frightened he was! He thought I was going to kill him. Why should I kill him? My hand trembled. And they've given me a St. George's Cross... I can't make it out at all."

But while Nicholas was pondering these questions and still couldn't reach a clear answer to what puzzled him so, the wheel of fortune in the service, as often happens, turned in his favor. After the action at Ostrovna he was brought to notice, given command of a hussar battalion, and whenever a brave officer was needed he was chosen.

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: On receiving news of Natasha's illness, the countess, though not quite well yet and still weak, went to Moscow with Petya and the rest of the household, and the whole family moved from Marya Dmitrievna's house to their own and settled in town.

Natasha's illness was so serious that, fortunately for her and for her parents, the question of all that had caused the illness — her conduct and the breaking off of her engagement — faded into the background. She was so ill that it was impossible for them to consider how far she was to blame for what had happened. She couldn't eat or sleep, grew visibly thinner, coughed, and as the doctors made them feel, was in danger. They could think of nothing but how to help her. Doctors came singly and in consultation, talked extensively in French, German, and Latin, blamed one another, and prescribed a great variety of medicines for all the diseases known to them, but the simple idea never occurred to any of them that they could not know the disease Natasha was suffering from, since no disease suffered by a living person can be known — for every living person has his own peculiarities and always has his own unique, personal, novel, complicated disease, unknown to medicine — not a disease of the lungs, liver, skin, heart, nerves, and so on listed in medical textbooks, but a disease consisting of one of the innumerable combinations of ailments of those organs. This simple thought could not occur to the doctors (as it cannot occur to a sorcerer that he is unable to work his spells) because the business of their lives was to cure, and they were paid for it, and had spent the best years of their lives in that business. But above all, this thought was kept from their minds by the fact that they saw they were genuinely useful — as indeed they were to the whole Rostov family. Their usefulness did not depend on making the patient swallow substances that were mostly harmful (the harm was scarcely perceptible, as they were given in small doses), but they were useful, necessary, and indispensable because they satisfied a mental need of the patient and of those who loved her — and that is why there are and always will be pseudo-healers, folk practitioners, homeopaths, and regular doctors. They satisfied that eternal human need for hope of relief, for sympathy, and for the feeling that something should be done — a need felt by those who are suffering. They satisfied the need seen in its most elementary form in a child: when it hurts itself and runs at once to the arms of its mother or nurse to have the sore spot rubbed or kissed, and it feels better when this is done. The child cannot believe that the strongest and wisest of its people have no remedy for its pain, and the hope of relief and the expression of its mother's sympathy while she rubs the bump comforts it. The doctors were of use to Natasha because they kissed and rubbed her bump, assuring her that it would soon pass if only the coachman went to the pharmacy on the Arbat and got a powder and some pills in a pretty box for a ruble and seventy kopecks, and if she took those powders in boiled water at intervals of precisely two hours, neither more nor less.

What would Sonya and the count and countess have done, how would they have looked, if nothing had been done — if there had not been those pills to give by the clock, the warm drinks, the chicken cutlets, and all the other details of life prescribed by the doctors, the carrying out of which gave occupation and comfort to the family? How would the count have borne his dearly loved daughter's illness had he not known that it was costing him a thousand rubles, and that he wouldn't grudge thousands more to help her, or had he not known that if her illness continued he wouldn't grudge yet more thousands and would take her abroad for consultations — and had he not been able to explain in detail how Metivier and Feller had not understood the symptoms, but Frise had, and Mudrov had diagnosed them even better? What would the countess have done had she not been able sometimes to scold the patient for not strictly obeying the doctor's orders?

"You'll never get well like that," she would say, forgetting her grief in her vexation, "if you won't follow the doctor and take your medicine at the right time! You mustn't trifle with it, you know, or it may turn to pneumonia," she would go on, drawing much comfort from the utterance of that foreign word, incomprehensible to others as well as to herself.

What would Sonya have done without the glad consciousness that she had not undressed during the first three nights so as to be ready to carry out all the doctor's instructions precisely, and that she still stayed awake at night so as not to miss the right time to administer the slightly harmful pills from the little gilt box? Even to Natasha herself it was pleasant to see that so many sacrifices were being made for her sake, and to know that she had to take medicine at certain hours, though she declared that no medicine would cure her and that it was all nonsense. And it was even satisfying to be able to show, by disregarding the instructions, that she didn't believe in medical treatment and didn't value her life.

The doctor came every day, felt her pulse, looked at her tongue, and regardless of her grief-stricken face, joked with her. But when he had gone into another room, to which the countess hurriedly followed him, he put on a grave expression and thoughtfully shaking his head said that though there was danger, he had hopes of the effect of this latest medicine, and that they must wait and see — that the illness was mainly psychological, but... And the countess, trying to hide the action from herself and from him, slipped a gold coin into his hand and always returned to the patient with a calmer mind.

The symptoms of Natasha's illness were that she ate little, slept little, coughed, and was always depressed. The doctors said she couldn't do without medical treatment, so they kept her in the stifling atmosphere of the city, and the Rostovs did not move to the country that summer of 1812.

In spite of the many pills she swallowed and the drops and powders from the little bottles and boxes — of which Madame Schoss, who was fond of such things, made a large collection — and in spite of being deprived of the country life she was used to, youth prevailed. Natasha's grief began to be overlaid by the impressions of daily life; it ceased to press so painfully on her heart, gradually faded into the past, and she began to recover physically.

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: Natasha was calmer but no happier. She didn't just avoid all outward forms of pleasure—balls, walks, concerts, and theaters—she never laughed without a trace of tears in her laughter. She couldn't sing. As soon as she started to laugh or tried to sing by herself, tears would choke her: tears of remorse, tears at the memory of those pure times that could never come back, tears of frustration that she had so uselessly ruined her young life, which might have been so happy. Laughing and singing especially felt like blasphemy in the face of her grief. Without needing any self-restraint, no desire to flirt ever entered her mind. She said and felt at that time that no man meant more to her than Nastasya Ivanovna, the household clown. Something stood guard inside her and forbade every joy. Besides, she had lost all the old interests of her carefree girlish life that had been so full of hope. The previous autumn—the hunting, "Uncle," and the Christmas holidays spent with Nicholas at Otradnoe—were what she recalled most often and most painfully. What wouldn't she have given to bring back even a single day of that time! But it was gone forever. Her feeling at the time had not deceived her—that state of freedom and readiness for any enjoyment would never return. Yet she had to go on living.

It comforted her to think that she was not better, as she had once imagined, but worse—much worse—than anybody else in the world. But this wasn't enough. She knew it, and asked herself, "What's next?" But there was nothing to come. There was no joy in life, yet life was passing. Natasha apparently tried not to be a burden or a hindrance to anyone, but wanted nothing for herself. She kept away from everyone in the house and felt at ease only with her brother Petya. She liked being with him better than with anyone else, and when alone with him she sometimes laughed. She hardly ever left the house, and of those who came to visit she was glad to see only one person—Pierre. It would have been impossible to treat her with more gentleness, greater care, and at the same time more seriousness than Count Bezukhov did. Natasha unconsciously felt this gentleness and so found great pleasure in his company. But she wasn't even grateful to him for it; nothing good on Pierre's part seemed like an effort—it seemed so natural for him to be kind to everyone that there was no merit in his kindness. Sometimes Natasha noticed embarrassment and awkwardness in him when he was around her, especially when he wanted to do something to please her or feared that something they were talking about would awaken painful memories. She noticed this and attributed it to his general kindness and shyness, which she imagined was the same toward everyone. After those involuntary words—that if he were free he would have asked on his knees for her hand and her love—spoken at a moment when she was so deeply shaken, Pierre never spoke to Natasha of his feelings; and it seemed obvious to her that those words, which had comforted her so much at the time, were spoken the way all sorts of meaningless things are said to comfort a crying child. It was not because Pierre was a married man, but because Natasha felt so strongly with him that moral barrier—the very barrier whose absence she had experienced with Kuragin—that it never entered her head that the relationship between them could lead to love on her part, still less on his, or even to the kind of tender, self-conscious, romantic friendship between a man and a woman of which she had known several examples.

Before the end of the fast of Saint Peter, Agrafena Ivanovna Belova, a country neighbor of the Rostovs, came to Moscow to pay her devotions at the shrines of the Moscow saints. She suggested that Natasha should fast and prepare for Holy Communion, and Natasha gladly welcomed the idea. Despite the doctor's orders that she should not go out early in the morning, Natasha insisted on fasting and preparing for the sacrament—not as they usually did in the Rostov family, by attending three services in their own house, but as Agrafena Ivanovna did, by going to church every day for a week and never missing Vespers, Matins, or Mass.

The countess was pleased with Natasha's devotion; after the poor results of the medical treatment, deep down she hoped that prayer might help her daughter more than medicine, and though not without fear and hiding it from the doctor, she agreed to Natasha's wish and entrusted her to Belova. Agrafena Ivanovna would come to wake Natasha at three in the morning, but generally found her already awake. She was afraid of being late for Matins. Hastily washing and humbly putting on her shabbiest dress and an old shawl, Natasha, shivering in the fresh air, went out into the deserted streets lit by the clear light of dawn. On Agrafena Ivanovna's advice, Natasha prepared herself not at their own parish church but at one where, according to the devout Agrafena Ivanovna, the priest was a man of very strict and lofty life. There were never many people in the church; Natasha always stood beside Belova in their customary place before an icon of the Blessed Virgin set into the screen before the choir on the left side, and a feeling new to her—of humility before something great and incomprehensible—seized her when, at that unusual morning hour, gazing at the dark face of the Virgin illuminated by the candles burning before it and by the morning light from the window, she listened to the words of the service and tried to follow them with understanding. When she understood them, her personal feelings became interwoven with the prayers in subtle ways of their own. When she did not understand, it was sweeter still to think that the desire to understand everything is pride, that it is impossible to understand all, that one only needs to believe and to surrender oneself to God, whom she felt guiding her soul in those moments. She crossed herself, bowed low, and when she didn't understand, in horror at her own sinfulness, simply asked God to forgive her for everything, everything, to have mercy on her. The prayers she surrendered to most fully were those of repentance. On her way home in the early hours, when she met no one but bricklayers going to work or men sweeping the street, and everybody in the houses was still asleep, Natasha experienced a new feeling—a sense of the possibility of correcting her faults, the possibility of a new, clean life, and of happiness.

Throughout the whole week she spent this way, that feeling grew every day. And the happiness of taking communion, or "communing" as Agrafena Ivanovna joyfully played with the word, seemed to Natasha so great that she felt she would never live to see that blessed Sunday.

But the happy day came, and on that memorable Sunday, when, dressed in white muslin, she returned home after communion, for the first time in many months she felt calm and no longer oppressed by the thought of the life that lay before her.
The doctor who came to see her that day ordered her to continue the powders he had prescribed two weeks earlier.
"She absolutely must keep taking them morning and evening," he said, clearly quite satisfied with his success. "Just be particular about it."

"Rest easy," he continued cheerfully, as he deftly slipped the gold coin into his palm. "She'll soon be singing and bouncing around. The last medicine has done her a world of good. She's freshened up wonderfully."
The countess, with a cheerful expression, looked down at her nails and gave a little spit for luck as she returned to the drawing room.

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: At the beginning of July, increasingly alarming reports about the war began to spread through Moscow; people spoke of an appeal by the Emperor to the people and of his coming in person from the army to Moscow. And since by the eleventh of July no manifesto or appeal had been received, exaggerated reports started circulating about them and about Russia's situation. It was said that the Emperor was leaving the army because it was in danger; it was said that Smolensk had surrendered, that Napoleon had an army of a million, and that only a miracle could save Russia.

On the eleventh of July, which was a Saturday, the manifesto was received but had not yet been printed, and Pierre, who was visiting the Rostovs, promised to come to dinner the next day, Sunday, and bring a copy of the manifesto and appeal, which he would get from Count Rostopchin.

That Sunday the Rostovs went to Mass at the Razumovskis' private chapel as usual. It was a hot July day. Even at ten o'clock, when the Rostovs got out of their carriage at the chapel, the sultry air, the shouts of street vendors, the light and cheerful summer clothes of the crowd, the dusty leaves of the trees on the boulevard, the sounds of the band and the white trousers of a battalion marching to parade, the rattling of wheels on the cobblestones, and the brilliant, hot sunshine were all full of that summer languor, that mix of contentment and discontent with the present, that is felt most strongly on a bright, hot day in town.
